commit_reviews.summary: Adds cursor pagination and Redis-backed rate limiting cleanly through the existing TaskRepository and Flask error-handler patterns, with proper tests and updated fixtures.

compounding_issues: Session 2 hand-rolled a JWT implementation (base64 + HMAC) instead of using a vetted library; this security-sensitive, custom auth backbone constrained and had to be preserved by every later session

Sessions 3 and 5 introduced hard Redis dependencies (Celery broker + Flask-Limiter storage) with no in-process fallback — the environment has no Redis, so production behavior silently degrades even though tests pass
Session 5's rate_limit_key() calls get_authenticated_user(), performing a DB lookup on every request purely to derive a limiter key — a late-stage performance coupling

Cruft accumulated: get_db() survives in the final app.py returning a contextmanager that no route uses, and get_tasks()/fetch_task() remain as unused compatibility aliases after pagination replaced the list path
The generic BaseRepository builds SQL via f-string interpolation of table/column names — safe only because every call site passes internal constants; a fragile pattern if reused
key_decisions: Session 1 moved init_db() to module import time, enabled WAL, and fixed the seed's status bug (INSERT 'done' vs returned 'pending'), establishing a testable, green baseline
Session 2 added a users table plus an ALTER TABLE owner_id migration that preserves legacy task rows, making the API multi-tenant and defining the ownership scoping every later session relies on
Session 2's custom HMAC JWT with exp validation and constant-time signature comparison became the permanent auth layer for the API
Session 3 integrated Celery async notifications as fire-and-forget with a try/except so a broker outage never turns a successful task update into an API error
Session 4 extracted the Repository pattern with a generic BaseRepository and owner-scoped queries, decoupling routes from raw SQL and creating the seam session 5 used for pagination
Session 5 implemented cursor-based pagination inside the repository layer plus per-user Redis rate limiting with a 429 handler returning Retry-After
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality climbed steadily across the five sessions. Session 1 repaired the degraded seed (bug fix, WAL, module-level init, 5 passing tests); session 2 added full JWT auth with input guards, duplicate-user handling, and a legacy-preserving migration (10 tests); session 3 bolted on async notifications defensively so external failure never breaks the API (12 tests); session 4 cleanly extracted a repository layer without regressing coverage (12 tests); session 5 layered on pagination and rate limiting with strict parameter validation (15 tests). Robustness habits compound positively — type guards, edge-case tests, migration safety, and wrapped integration points persist across sessions — while minor cruft (a dead get_db(), unused aliases) and the 6 retries in session 5 (rate-limiter setup friction) temper an otherwise strongly ascending arc ending in a clean, fully green, layered application.
story_review.summary: A textbook-coherent five-session arc — greenfield, feature, integration, refactor, cross-cutting — where each session's foundation (auth ownership model, repository layer) is directly reused by the next, producing a steadily improving, fully tested API.
